blocks.prompt: The Brush That Drinks the Paint
blocks.text: A paintbrush has three parts. The handle is the long stick you hold. The ferrule is the shiny metal ring in the middle. Say it FER-rul. The hairs are called bristles. The ferrule holds the bristles tight so they do not fall out. When you dip the brush, paint sneaks into the tiny gaps between the bristles and stays there. That is why one dip can draw a long line. When you press down, the bristles bend and the paint slides onto the paper. Wash your brush when you are done. Then the paint will not dry hard inside.

blocks.prompt: Three Parts and a Tiny Trick
blocks.text: Every paintbrush is made of three parts. The handle is the part you hold. The bristles are the hairs at the tip. Between them sits a metal tube called the ferrule, which grips the bristles and clamps onto the handle. The clever part is how a brush carries paint. The bristles are not glued into one solid lump. They are packed side by side with tiny gaps between them. When you dip the brush, paint creeps up into those gaps and stays. Scientists call this capillary action. It is the same reason a paper towel soaks up a spill. The brush is not just a tool. It is a small tank. Press the brush on paper and the bristles bend and spread. Paint leaves the gaps and sticks to the paper instead. Lift the brush and the bristles spring back into shape. A good brush can do this thousands of times. That is also why you never leave a brush standing on its tip in a jar. The bristles bend and never come back straight.

blocks.prompt: The Tank on a Stick
blocks.text: A paintbrush looks like the simplest tool in the art box. It is not. It is a small, carefully engineered tank. Start with the three parts. The handle balances the brush in your hand. The ferrule, the metal tube near the tip, crimps onto the handle and holds the hairs in a bed of glue. The hairs themselves do the work. Those hairs are chosen, not just cut. Natural brushes use hog bristle, goat, squirrel, or sable, the tail hair of a weasel called the kolinsky. Each kind behaves differently. Hog bristle is stiff and springy and pushes thick paint around. Its tips split naturally into little forks called flags, and the forks grab more paint. Sable is soft, holds a needle point, and snaps back to shape after every stroke. Squirrel hair holds a huge amount of water but has almost no spring. Synthetic brushes copy these hairs with tapered plastic filaments. The physics is the interesting part. Paint does not sit on the outside of a brush. It hides in the narrow channels between the hairs, pulled in and held there by capillary action, the same force that walks water up a paper towel. Press down and the hairs splay apart, the channels open, and paint releases onto the paper. Lift, and the hairs close and hold the rest back. That is also why water is the enemy of the ferrule. Soak a brush and water creeps past the hairs, swells the wooden handle, and softens the glue. The brush starts shedding, and no amount of careful painting brings it back.

blocks.prompt: The Most Underrated Tool in the Room
blocks.text: Ask most people to name a piece of technology and they point at a screen. Almost nobody points at a paintbrush. They should. Look closely at a good round watercolor brush. It comes to a point so fine you could sign your name with it, and here is the surprising part: nobody cut that point. Every hair in the bundle is naturally tapered, thick through the middle and fine at the tip, and a brush maker sorts the hairs by hand, stands them upright in a small metal cup so the tips settle level, and ties the bundle before it ever meets a ferrule. Cutting the hairs would ruin the brush. A cut hair has a blunt end, and a bundle of blunt ends cannot make a point. The bundle then does something no solid tool can do. It stores liquid. Paint is pulled into the narrow spaces between the hairs by capillary action and held there against gravity. The wide middle of the bundle, which brush makers call the belly, works as a reservoir. Your fingers control the rest. Press, and the hairs splay, the channels widen, and paint flows out. Ease off, and the channels close and the brush keeps what is left for the next stroke. One dip can draw a line the length of your arm. The shape of the brush rewrote art history. For centuries brushes were round, because the only good way to bind hairs was to thread them into a bird quill, and quills are round. Then, in the early 1800s, brush makers began fitting hairs into a flattened metal ferrule. The flat brush was born, and with it the broad, loaded, visible stroke. Around the same time, an American painter named John Goffe Rand invented the collapsible metal paint tube. Suddenly an artist could carry paint outdoors and lay it on thick with a flat brush. The Impressionists did exactly that. Their loose, visible brushwork was not only a new idea about seeing. It was also a new idea about hardware. Every trade has its own brush. A house painter's brush is wide and stiff. A calligrapher in China writes with a soft brush of goat or weasel hair that has been made in much the same way for more than two thousand years. A model painter uses a brush with barely a dozen hairs in it. Same three parts. Same trick. Different job.

Kolinsky sable: tail hair of a Siberian weasel

blocks.prompt: The Valve at the End of a Stick
blocks.text: There is a good argument that the paintbrush is the most underrated machine ever built. It has no moving parts in the way an engine does, and yet it solves a problem that sounds impossible when you state it plainly: pick up a measured quantity of liquid, carry it through the air without dropping it, and then release it, in a controlled amount, exactly where you decide. The solution is geometry. A brush is not a lump of hair. It is a bundle of hairs held just far enough apart that the gaps between them become channels. Liquid entering those channels is caught by two forces at once: adhesion, which makes water molecules cling to the hair, and cohesion, which makes them cling to each other. Together they produce capillary action, the same effect that walks a spill up a paper towel and climbs water up the inside of a narrow glass tube. The thickest part of the bundle, which brush makers call the belly, is a reservoir. The tip is a nozzle. Your fingers are the throttle. Press, and the hairs splay, the channels widen, and paint leaves. Ease off, and the channels narrow and hold the rest back. A painter is not pushing paint. A painter is operating a valve. The craft is in the hair. A fine round brush comes to a point sharp enough to draw a line thinner than a pencil could, and the point is not cut. It cannot be cut. Each natural hair is already tapered along its length, fat through the middle and fine at the end, and a brush maker's job is to sort hairs by length and quality, stand them upright in a metal cup until the tips settle into a common curve, and bind the bundle without disturbing them. Cut the tips off and you get a bundle of blunt stumps that will never converge. Different hairs sell different behaviors. Hog bristle is coarse and stiff, and its ends split naturally into flags, small forks that grab thick oil paint and drag it across canvas. Kolinsky sable, taken from the tail of a Siberian weasel, is soft but has extraordinary snap: bend it and it returns to a needle point every single time. Squirrel is softer still and carries enormous volumes of water while offering almost no spring at all. Modern synthetic filaments are extruded from nylon or polyester and tapered by machine, and the good ones are now hard to tell apart from the animal they imitate. Hardware shapes art more often than art historians like to admit. For most of recorded history brushes were round, for an unglamorous reason: the best way to bind a bundle of hair was to thread it into a bird's quill, and a quill is a tube. In the early nineteenth century, brush makers began crimping hair into flattened metal ferrules. The flat brush arrived, and with it a stroke that was wide, heavily loaded, and unashamedly visible. In 1841 an American painter, John Goffe Rand, patented a collapsible metal tube for paint, which meant that for the first time paint could travel. Put those two objects in the same bag and you can walk into a field with a flat brush and a pocket of ready color and paint the light before it moves. The Impressionists did precisely that. Their revolution is usually explained as a new theory of perception. It was also a new toolkit. None of this is new. People were painting the walls of caves at least thirty thousand years ago, using chewed sticks, pads of moss and fur, bare fingers, and pigment blown through hollow bone. Every brush since has been another answer to the identical question those hands were asking. Hold a liquid. Carry it. Let it go on purpose.
